newsitem.title: UK: POLL -British interest rates seen peaking in Q2 1998.
newsitem.headline: POLL -British interest rates seen peaking in Q2 1998.

text.p: Britain's official interest rates, raised three times over the past three months, are expected to creep further upwards over the next year before easing back to current levels, a Reuters survey showed on Monday.

In a quarterly poll of British economic indicators, exchange and interest rates, the median of up to 25 forecasts showed that the current base rate cycle would peak at 7.20 percent at the end of June next year. The forecasts ranged from six to 8.5 percent.
The survey found that after the mid-year peak during 1998, rates were then expected to ease. The survey's median forecast for June 1999 was 6.50 percent, with a range of 5.25 to 7.75 percent.
The poll was conducted between July 7 and 9, before the Bank of England's (BoE) monetary policy committee agreed last Thursday to raise rates by 25 basis points to 6.75 percent.
Twenty-nine banks, investment and research houses provided forecasts for the quarterly survey.
Analysts said they expected the central bank to continue a policy of small, regular rate increases.
"It is likely that the BoE will now hold off from moving rates at the next meeting, but risks on rates are for the upside," said Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marian Bell.
"We would certainly expect a seven percent base rate by the end of this quarter," said Bank America's Jeremy Hawkins.

"As long as the forex market has something to look forward to, it's unlikely to offload its positions. By the year end we will be looking at a rate of 7.25 percent," said Paribas economist Nick Parsons.

"The danger is that (the Bank of England) may be rebalancing the economy but at lower levels of growth and output. We may have to be dusting off the "R" word, the recession word, as manufacturing slows down next year," he added.

The BoE is faced with juggling the need for higher rates to control consumer spending, which has recently been boosted by 30 billion sterling of windfall payments from building society flotations, with the need to prevent another surge in sterling, which could further hurt UK exports.
"The Bank of England is still opting for a gradualist approach and trying to minimise the adverse effects on the pound and output," said DKB chief economist Gerard Lyons.
The central bank's duty is to ensure Britain keeps to the new Labour government's official target of 2.5 percent inflation.
Sterling was buoyed early this month by the government's first budget which did little do dampen the windfall-driven consumer demand.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown handed over control of monetary policy to the central bank shortly after the May 1 election and analysts said his budget showed he expected the central bank to use its powers to prevent the economy overheating.
